sources.says: Rashi, explaining the root on Exodus, says the חרוץ of this verse is a sharp, keen man.

sources.quote: חרוץ. זרוז וישר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means quick and upright.

21:9.headline: A shared house, or a Temple where an idol shares God's place
21:9.body: Plainly, בית חבר is a house shared with a quarrelsome wife, as Ibn Ezra reads it. Rashi also gives a deeper reading: a house where partners are joined to God, like the idol King Manasseh set up in the Temple.

sources.quote: כלומר ובית חברה, כלומר שיהיה לו בית להתחבר עמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means a house he has to share with her.

sources.quote: בַּיִת שֶׁמְּחַבְּרִים בּוֹ רֵעִים לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּגוֹן צֶלֶם שֶׁהֶעֱמִיד מְנַשֶּׁה בְּהֵיכַל ה׳
sources.says: Rashi says it is a house where companions are joined to God, like the idol Manasseh set up in God's Temple.

21:12.headline: The Righteous One here may be God himself
21:12.body: Rashi says the צדיק here is the Righteous One of the world, God, who sets his mind to cut off the house of the wicked. Ralbag reads it as a righteous person whose presence brings success to a wicked man's house.

sources.quote: צַדִּיקוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, נוֹתֵן לֵב לְהַכְרִית בֵּית רָשָׁע
sources.says: Rashi says the righteous one is the Righteous One of the world, God, who sets his heart on cutting off the house of the wicked.

sources.quote: הצדיק המצליח לבית הרשע וזה יהיה כשיעמוד בביתו
sources.says: Ralbag says it is a righteous man who brings success to the wicked man's house when he stays there.

21:14.headline: A bribe in the lap, read as quiet charity
21:14.body: שחד usually means a bribe. Rashi reads both the secret gift and the 'bribe in the lap' as charity. Ralbag reads it plainly: a quiet gift calms someone who is angry with you.

sources.quote: מַתָּן בַּסֵּתֶר. צְדָקָה
sources.says: Rashi says the gift in secret is charity.

sources.quote: וְשֹׁחַד בַּחֵק. אַף זוֹ צְדָקָה
sources.says: Rashi says the bribe in the lap is also charity.

sources.quote: הנה המתן שיתן האדם בסתר למי שיכעס עליו מכניע האף והחמה
sources.says: Ralbag says a gift given in secret to someone angry with you subdues his anger.

21:14.headline: A secret gift bends anger down, or covers it over
21:14.body: Ibn Ezra reads יכפה as bending down, like יכפף. Metzudat Zion reads it as covering, like the Sages' phrase about God holding the mountain over Israel like a tub.

sources.quote: יכפה - פירוש ישפיל, כמו יכפף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'lowers', like the word for bending.

sources.quote: יכפה. ענין כסוי ובדרז״ל כפה עליהם הר כגיגית
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means covering, as in the Sages' saying that God held the mountain over them like a tub.

21:16.headline: The Refaim are the dead, named for their weakness
21:16.body: רפאים here means the dead. Metzudat Zion says they are called this because they have gone slack and weak, from רפה. Rashi says their company is the company of Gehinnom.

sources.quote: רפאים. הם המתים שנרפו ונחלשו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Refaim are the dead, who have gone slack and weak.

sources.quote: בִּקְהַל רְפָאִים. בַּעֲדַת גֵּיהִנֹּם
sources.says: Rashi says the assembly of the Refaim is the company of Gehinnom.

21:21.headline: Honor, or wealth: כבוד also carries the sense of weight
21:21.body: Ibn Ezra says כבוד here may mean that people will honor him. Or it may mean money, from כבד מאד, 'very heavy', a phrase for being rich.

sources.quote: וכבוד – שיכבדוהו בני אדם, או יתן לו כבוד השם, כלומר ממון מן כבד מאוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means people will honor him, or that God will give him wealth, from 'very heavy'.

21:29.headline: His face here means his anger, because anger shows
21:29.body: פנים usually means face. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it here as anger. Metzudat Zion explains that anger shows on a person's face, and points to a verse about Hannah in Samuel.

sources.quote: בְּפָנָיו. מִלְּשׁוֹן ״אַף״
sources.says: Rashi says the word has the sense of anger.

sources.quote: הָרָשָׁע מַרְאֶה עַזּוּתוֹ בִּשְׁעַת כַּעֲסוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the wicked man shows his boldness when he is angry.

sources.quote: בפניו. בכעסו וכן ופניה לא היה לה (שמואל א א) כי הכעס נראה בפני האדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'in his anger', because anger shows on a person's face.

22:4.headline: Humility's 'heel': what it brings, or what sits under it?
22:4.body: עקב means heel, and also 'because of' or 'the end of'. Rashi first reads: because of humility, fear of God comes. His second reading keeps the heel: humility is the main thing, and fear of God is the heel under its foot.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁבִיל הָעֲנָוָה יִרְאַת ה׳ בָּאָה
sources.says: Rashi says that because of humility, fear of God comes.

sources.quote: עֲנָוָה עִקָּר, וְהַיִּרְאָה טְפֵלָה וְעָקֵב לָהּ, מִדְרָס לְרַגְלֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi's second reading says humility is the main thing, and fear of God is secondary, a heel and a footrest for it.

sources.quote: עניינו סוף ואחרית ע״ש שהעקב הוא סוף הרגל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the end, because the heel is the end of the foot.

22:5.headline: Thorns, bandits, or cold on the crooked road?
22:5.body: צנים can mean thorns, and Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read it that way. Rashi ties it to a word for armed troops: bands of robbers waiting on the crooked man's road. Ralbag reads it as cold that harms him.

sources.quote: צנים. קוצים כמו ולצנינים בצדיכם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means thorns, as in 'thorns in your sides' in Numbers 33.

sources.quote: צנים - שרשו צנן מן ולצנינים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says its root is the one in 'thorns in your sides'.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן גְּדוּדִים וְלִסְטִים
sources.says: Rashi says the word means troops and bandits.

sources.quote: ימצא צנים להנזק בקרירות האויר
sources.says: Ralbag says the crooked man meets צנים and is harmed by the cold air.

22:6.headline: Teach a child, or start him on a path he will keep?
22:6.body: חנך is also the word for dedicating a new house. Metzudat Zion says it means starting something that will last. Ibn Ezra reads it as teaching, like Abraham's trained men. Rashi warns that it cuts both ways: what a child starts on, good or bad, he keeps.

sources.quote: הוא ענין התחלה לדבר שעתיד לעמוד בו כמו ולא חנכו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means beginning something a person will stay with, as in dedicating a new house in Deuteronomy 20.

sources.quote: חנוך - למד, כמו: חניכיו כלומר מלומדי כלי מלחמה שלו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to teach, as Abraham's חניכים were men trained in weapons.

sources.quote: אִם לְטוֹב אִם לְרַע, גַּם כִּי יַזְקִין לֹא יָסוּר מִמֶּנָּה
sources.says: Rashi says whatever you train the child in, good or bad, he will not leave it even when old.

22:14.headline: The mouth of strange women, or of strange worship?
22:14.body: זרות means strangers, here women. Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: the talk of a seductive woman is a deep pit. Rashi reads it as the mouth of idol worshippers, and Metzudat David as heresy, which is hard to climb out of.

sources.quote: כשוחה שהיא עמוקה כן פי נשים זרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the mouth of strange women is like a deep pit.

sources.quote: שׁוּחָה עֲמֻקָּה פִּי זָרוֹת. פִּי עוֹבְדֵי גִּלּוּלִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is the mouth of idol worshippers.

sources.quote: היא המינות אשר יקשה מאוד לפרוש ממנה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is heresy, which is very hard to leave.

22:20.headline: Written 'day before yesterday', read 'noble things' or 'three parts'
22:20.body: The written text has שלשום, 'the day before yesterday', and the reading is שלישים. Ibn Ezra follows the written form: I wrote to you before. Rashi reads three: Torah, Prophets and Writings. Metzudat Zion reads officers, as in Exodus 15: weighty, noble words.

sources.quote: אתמול שלשום כתבתי להודיעך אמרי אמת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'before now I wrote to you' words of truth.

sources.quote: הֲלֹא כָתַבְתִּי לְךָ שָׁלִשִׁים. תּוֹרָה וּנְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים
sources.says: Rashi says the three things written are the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings.

sources.quote: שרים ונכבדים כמו ומבחר שלישיו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means officers and nobles, as in 'his chosen officers' in Exodus 15, so weighty and noble words.

sources.quote: וְהָא כִּתְבֵת אִנוּן לָךְ עַל תְּלָתָא זִמְנִין
sources.says: The Targum translates 'I have written them for you three times'.

22:28.headline: Don't move the old boundary stone, or the old custom
22:28.body: Metzudat David reads it plainly: do not shift the marker between your field and your neighbor's. Rashi reads it as your fathers' custom too. He cites the sages: a basket set under the vine to catch the fallen grapes, which belong to the poor, moves the boundary.

sources.quote: סימן הגבול אשר מעולם אשר עשו אבותיך אל תחזיר לאחור אל תוך שדה רעך
sources.says: Metzudat David says do not push the old boundary marker back into your neighbor's field.

sources.quote: אַל תָּשֵׁג אָחוֹר מִנְהַג אֲבוֹתֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says do not move back from your fathers' custom.

sources.quote: הַמַּנִּיחַ כַּלְכָּלָה תַּחַת הַגֶּפֶן בִּשְׁעַת בְּצִירָה כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּפּוֹל בְּתוֹכוֹ הַפֶּרֶט
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: one who puts a basket under the vine at harvest to catch the fallen grapes breaks this verse.

sources.quote: וזאת ג"כ הערה שלא ישנה הגדרים הקודמים שגדרו הראשונים
sources.says: Ralbag says the verse also hints not to change the fences set by earlier generations.

22:29.headline: Lowly people are called 'dark', as nobles are called 'white'
22:29.body: חשכים means lowly people. Metzudat Zion explains the word: nobles are called חורים, from 'white', so the lowly are called חשוכים, from 'dark'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the poor, as the Aramaic uses it.

sources.quote: כי כמו שנקראים שרים חורים מל׳ חיור ולובן כן יקראו הפחותים חשוכים מל׳ חושך ושחרות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says just as nobles are called חורים from 'white', the lowly are called חשוכים from 'darkness'.

sources.quote: חשוכים - עניים, ותרגום: דלות חשיכן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means the poor, as the Aramaic translation uses the word.

23:2.headline: A man of big appetite, or a man in control of himself
23:2.body: בעל נפש can point two ways. Rashi reads it as a hungry, greedy eater, while the Targum translates "master of your soul" and Metzudat David reads it as a person with a thinking soul who rejects what is bad.

sources.quote: אִם רַעַבְתָּן אַתָּה וְתָאֵב לֶאֱכוֹל
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'if you are a glutton and eager to eat'.

sources.quote: אִין מָרָא דְנַפְשָׁךְ אָתְּ
sources.says: The Targum translates 'if you are master of your soul'.

sources.quote: אם יש לך נפש משכלת למאוס ברע
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means if you have a thinking soul that rejects what is bad.

23:4.headline: Do not wear yourself out getting rich, or cramming
23:4.body: Ralbag reads the warning plainly: chasing wealth uses up the time you need for wisdom. Rashi reads "getting rich" as piling up learning in great bundles, which you will end up forgetting.

sources.quote: כי זה ימנע לך מבינתך בסבת כלוי זמנך בענין העושר
sources.says: Ralbag says chasing wealth keeps you from understanding, because it uses up your time.

sources.quote: לַעֲשׂוֹת גִּירְסָתְךָ חֲבִילוֹת חֲבִילוֹת, כִּי סוֹף שֶׁתִּשְׁכָּחֶנָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means do not heap up your learning in bundles, since in the end you will forget it.

23:7.headline: A gate, a reckoning, or a bitter taste
23:7.body: The Targum keeps the usual sense, gate: the host is high in his own eyes like a tall gate. Ibn Ezra reads it as measuring out, and Rashi, from the rotten figs in Jeremiah, as bitterness poured into the stingy host's soul.

sources.quote: דְאֵיךְ תַּרְעָא רָמֵא הָכֵן הוּא רָם בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ
sources.says: The Targum translates 'like a high gate, so is he high in his soul'.

sources.quote: שער - פועל עבר מן מאה שערים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a verb meaning to measure, as in 'a hundredfold': the host measures out in his mind what you eat.

sources.quote: כְּאִלּוּ שָׁפַךְ הָאוֹכֵל הַזֶּה מְרָה בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל רַע הָעַיִן
sources.says: Rashi says the vowels show it is a verb, from the 'rotten figs' in Jeremiah: your eating is like bitterness poured into the stingy man's soul.

23:10.headline: An ancient boundary, or the boundary of the poor
23:10.body: Metzudat David reads גבול עולם as a boundary set long ago. Malbim reads עולם as "everyone": the share of every field that belongs to the poor, and Rashi speaks of the gleanings due to orphans.

sources.quote: אל תחזיר לאחור סימן הגבול הנעשה מעולם
sources.says: Metzudat David says do not move back a boundary marker set up long ago.

sources.quote: שהוא הגבול המיוחד לעניים בכל העולם ללקט את מתנותיהם
sources.says: Malbim says, following the Sifra, that this is the boundary set aside for the poor everywhere, to gather their gifts.

sources.quote: בְּלֶקֶט שִׁכְחָה וּפֵאָה הָרָאוּי לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the orphans' fields means the gleanings and corners of the field that are theirs by right.

23:11.headline: The orphans' redeemer is God himself
23:11.body: A גואל is the close relative with the right to buy back a family's land, as Malbim explains. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say the orphans' strong redeemer here is God.

sources.quote: שגדר הגואל הוא הקרוב שלו משפט הגאולה
sources.says: Malbim says a redeemer is the relative who holds the right of redemption.

sources.quote: כי השם שהוא גואלם שיגאל השדה מידך חזק הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God is their redeemer, who will take the field back from you, and he is strong.

sources.quote: הלא ה׳ הגואל אותם הוא חזק
sources.says: Metzudat David says that though the orphans are weak, God who redeems them is strong.

23:16.headline: Rejoicing kidneys: where the Bible feels joy
23:16.body: The father says his kidneys will rejoice. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra explain that desire and joy were felt in the kidneys, and Malbim adds that the heart thinks while the kidneys give counsel.

sources.quote: כליותי. תאות השמחה היא בכליות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the desire for joy is in the kidneys.

sources.quote: כליותי - מן: כלתה לישועתך, כי מדת התאוה בהם נודעת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra ties the word to longing, as in 'my soul longs for your salvation', since desire is known to sit in the kidneys.

sources.quote: הלב חושב והכליות יועצות
sources.says: Malbim quotes the saying that the heart thinks and the kidneys advise, so their joy is closer to action.

23:19.headline: Walk your heart straight, or down the road to happiness
23:19.body: Metzudat Zion reads ואשר from אשור, a footstep: walk your heart along the path. Malbim reads it from אושר, happiness: lead your heart down the road to lasting good.

sources.quote: ואשר. ענין מצעדים ופסיעות כמו ואשרו בדרך בינה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means steps and strides, as in an earlier verse about walking in understanding.

sources.quote: ואשר, פעל זה בא על ההולך בדרך האושר הנפשיי
sources.says: Malbim says this verb is used for walking the road of the soul's happiness.

sources.quote: וְתָרֵץ לִבָּךְ לְאָרְחָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'and set your heart straight on the way'.

23:20.headline: Gluttons for themselves, or eating their own flesh
23:20.body: The verse ends with the short word למו, "for them". Metzudat David reads it as eating for their own pleasure, not to honor Sabbath and holidays, while Malbim suggests a picture: gluttons who end up eating away their own flesh.

sources.quote: ר״ל להנאת עצמם לא לענג שבתות וי״ט
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means for their own pleasure, not to honor Sabbaths and festivals.

sources.quote: על צד המליצה שזוללים בשר עצמם
sources.says: Malbim says it can be read as a figure of speech: they devour their own flesh.

23:23.headline: Buy truth and do not sell it: do not teach for pay
23:23.body: Rashi brings the Sages' reading: if you must, pay to learn, but do not then charge others to learn from you. Malbim reads it as not buying truth like a trader who means to resell it, studying only for wealth or honor.

sources.quote: וְאַל תֹּאמַר: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁלָּמַדְתִּי בְּשָׂכָר, כָּךְ אֲלַמְּדֶנָּה בְּשָׂכָר
sources.says: Rashi says if you cannot learn for free, learn for pay, but do not say 'as I paid to learn, so I will charge to teach'.

sources.quote: ועכ״ז אל תמכור ללמדה לאחרים בשכר
sources.says: Metzudat David says even so, do not sell it by teaching others for pay.

sources.quote: שלא תקנהו כסוחר הקונה
sources.says: Malbim says do not acquire truth like a merchant who buys to resell, studying for wealth or honor.

23:24.headline: Who "begets" a wise son: his father or his teacher?
23:24.body: Metzudat David reads the one who begets a wise son as his teacher, who gives birth to wisdom in a student's heart. Malbim says the reverse: אב, father, can include a teacher, but יולד means only the man who fathered him.

sources.quote: המוליד את החכם ר״ל המלמד ומוליד חכמה בלב התלמיד
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the teacher, who gives birth to wisdom in the student's heart.

sources.quote: שהאב כולל גם האומן אותו והמורהו, אבל המוליד הוא דוקא אביו אשר ילדו
sources.says: Malbim says 'father' also covers the one who raised and taught him, but 'begetter' means only his natural father.

23:26.headline: Your eyes will keep my ways, or run along them
23:26.body: The word is read תצרנה, "they will keep", but written תרצנה with the letters swapped. Ibn Ezra reads the written form as running: your eyes will run along the ways of the commandments.

sources.quote: תצרנה - תרצנה כתיב, ופירוש עיניך ירוצו דרכי המצות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes it is written תרצנה, and explains that your eyes will run in the ways of the commandments.

sources.quote: וְעַיְנָךְ תִּנְטְרָן אָרְחָתָי
sources.says: The Targum translates the read form: 'and your eyes will guard my ways'.

23:27.headline: The foreign woman may stand for heresy
23:27.body: Plainly the verse warns against the harlot and the foreign woman. Malbim reads the harlot as desire and the foreign woman as heresy, and Rashi and Metzudat David also read these verses as speaking of heresy.

sources.quote: כי הנכריה שהיא המינות, דומה כבאר צרה
sources.says: Malbim says the foreign woman is heresy, like a narrow well where one who falls in drowns.

sources.quote: ונאמר למשל על המינות
sources.says: Metzudat David says the image is also said as a parable about heresy.

sources.quote: וְעַל הָאֲפִיקוֹרְסִין מְדַבֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says the next verse is speaking about heretics who lead people to betray God.

23:29.headline: A cry of grief, of poverty, or of craving
23:29.body: אבוי is a rare word. Rashi hears a cry of wailing, Ibn Ezra ties it to אביון, a poor man, and Malbim to אבה, wanting: whoever craves will end up crying אוי.

sources.quote: לְמִי אוֹי לְמִי אֲבוֹי. לְשׁוֹן צְעָקָה וִילָלָה
sources.says: Rashi says both words are cries of wailing.

sources.quote: אבוי - שם דבר מן אביון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a noun from אביון, a poor man.

sources.quote: אבוי. שרשו אבה, התאוה והחפץ
sources.says: Malbim says its root is אבה, desire and wanting.

23:31.headline: Written "in the pocket", read "in the cup"
23:31.body: The word is read בכוס, "in the cup", but written בכיס, "in the pocket". Rashi brings the Sages' play: the drinker has his eye on the cup, and the wine seller has his eye on the drinker's pocket.

sources.quote: בַּכִּיס כְּתִיב, כְּלוֹמַר: הַשּׁוֹתֶה נוֹתֵן עַיִן בַּכּוֹס וְהַחֶנְוָנִי – בְּכִיסוֹ שֶׁל זֶה
sources.says: Rashi notes it is written 'in the pocket': the drinker eyes the cup and the shopkeeper eyes the drinker's pocket.

23:32.headline: The viper stings, cuts off life, or spreads poison
23:32.body: יפרש is a rare verb. Rashi reads it as stinging, like an ox goad, or as cutting a man off from life, while Malbim reads it from פרש, dung: a snake whose very waste is poison.

sources.quote: יַפְרִישׁ. לְשׁוֹן עֲקִיצָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means stinging, like the ox goad in Judges, and that some read it as separating him from life.

sources.quote: המפריש חיי האדם ממנו ע״י ארסו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it separates a man's life from him with its venom.

sources.quote: יפריש. פעל משם פרש, שמורה על הצואה
sources.says: Malbim says it is a verb from פרש, dung, for a snake whose waste is poisonous.

sources.quote: ומזה הענין נקרא פרש בעבור הפרישין אשר ברגליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to pierce, and that a horseman is called פרש for the spurs on his feet.

23:33.headline: Your heart will speak: speech that is only thought
23:33.body: דבר usually means to speak aloud. Maimonides lists this verse among those where speaking means a thought formed in the mind and never said.

sources.quote: ויש לו הוראה של העניין המצטייר
sources.says: Maimonides says speaking can mean an idea pictured in the mind without being said, and cites 'your heart will speak' from this verse.

23:33.headline: Strange sights, or strange women
23:33.body: זרות means strange things. Ibn Ezra and Rashi say the drunk's eyes go to strange women, while Metzudat David and Ralbag say he sees things that are not there at all.

sources.quote: זרות - חסר, כלומר יראו נשים זרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a word is missing: your eyes will look at strange women.

sources.quote: הַיַּיִן בּוֹעֵר בְּךָ וּמַשִּׂיאֲךָ לְהַבִּיט בְּזוֹנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the wine burns in you and leads you to look at harlots.

sources.quote: כי מרוב השכרות ידמה שרואה דבר מה ואין כל מאומה
sources.says: Metzudat David says from heavy drinking he imagines he sees something when nothing is there.

sources.quote: דברים שאינם כן מצד רוב האידים העולים אל המוח
sources.says: Ralbag says drunkenness shows you things that are not so, because of vapors rising to the brain.

23:34.headline: Lying at the top of the mast
23:34.body: חבל here is a rare word. Rashi and Metzudat David say it is the ship's mast, where all the ropes hang, while Ibn Ezra says it is the rope tied to the ship's iron.

sources.quote: תֹּרֶן הַסְּפִינָה נוֹחַ לִפּוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the ship's mast, from which it is easy to fall.

sources.quote: הוא תורן הספינה שכל החבלים תלוים בו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is the mast, on which all the ropes hang.

sources.quote: חבל - שם והוא החבל שקשור בברזל הספינה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a noun meaning the rope tied to the ship's iron.

24:16.headline: Seven times means many times, not an exact count
24:16.body: Metzudat Zion and Meiri say שבע, seven, is a way of saying 'many'. A righteous person falls again and again and gets up each time, as Ralbag puts it.

sources.quote: שבע. ר״ל הרבה וכן שבע יפול צדיק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says seven means 'many', and cites this verse.

sources.quote: ר״ל הרבה פעמים הללתיך ואין מנין השבע בדיוק
sources.says: Meiri says seven means many times and is not an exact number, and cites this verse as the same usage.

sources.quote: הצדיק יפול פעמים רבות ויקום בכל פעם ופעם
sources.says: Ralbag says the righteous man falls many times and gets up every time.

24:20.headline: The lamp of the wicked goes out, its flame leaping away
24:20.body: ידעך means to go out. Metzudat Zion says the word pictures leaping: when a lamp goes out, the flame jumps off the wick.

sources.quote: ידעך. ענין ניתר וקפיצה כמו דועכו כאש קוצים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means leaping and jumping, as in 'they were put out like a fire of thorns'.

sources.quote: כבוי הנר שקופץ השלהבת מן הפתילה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a lamp goes out when the flame jumps off the wick.

25:1.headline: Hezekiah's men copied Solomon's sayings, or held on to them
25:1.body: העתיקו usually means to move something from its place. Metzudat Zion says copying from book to book took this name because the words seem to move, while Rashi reads it as "they took hold of" the sayings.

sources.quote: כותב הדברים מספר אל ספר יקרא מעתיק לפי שנראה כאלו מעתיק ומסיר הדברים משם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says one who copies from book to book is called a mover, because it looks as if he takes the words away from there.

sources.quote: הֶעְתִּיקוּ. הֶחֱזִיקוּ
sources.says: Rashi explains the word as 'they took hold of'.

sources.quote: דִכְתָבוּ רַחֲמוֹי דְחִזְקְיָה
sources.says: The Targum translates 'which the friends of Hezekiah wrote down'.

25:10.headline: Here חסד means shame, not kindness
25:10.body: חסד usually means kindness. Here, as in one verse in Leviticus, it means disgrace: whoever hears you reveal a secret will shame you as a gossip.

sources.quote: פֶּן יְחַסֶּדְךָ, הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ וְיִקְרָאֲךָ מוֹצִיא דִּבָּה
sources.says: Rashi notes the Targum renders 'the shame of Egypt' with this root, and says the listener will call you a slanderer.

sources.quote: יחסדך. ענין חרפה כמו חסד הוא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means disgrace, as in the verse in Leviticus that calls a forbidden union חסד.

sources.quote: פן יחסדך - יחרפך שומע ויקראך רכיל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the listener will shame you and call you a talebearer.

25:11.headline: Gold apples seen through a silver screen
25:11.body: משכיות is a rare word. Rashi reads it as vessels covered in silver, while Ralbag and Malbim see silver work with tiny holes, so the gold shows through, the way a deeper meaning shows through a well-made saying.

sources.quote: מַשְׂכִּיּוֹת כֵּלִים הַמְצֻפִּין בְּכֶסֶף, כְּמוֹ ״וְשַׂכֹּתִי כַפִּי״
sources.says: Rashi says they are vessels plated with silver, from the word for covering, as in 'I will cover you with my hand'.

sources.quote: במשכיות כסף שיש בהם נקבים דקים יראה דק העיון מהם תפוחי הזהב
sources.says: Ralbag says the silver has fine holes, and a careful looker sees the gold apples through them, as a careful thinker finds the inner meaning of a saying.

sources.quote: שדרך הנקבים של הציפוי יביט את הזהב הנסתר תחתיו
sources.says: Malbim says the word is from 'looking', and here means silver work through whose holes one sees the hidden gold.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Prefatory Remarks 20
sources.quote: מאפייני המשל העשוי כהלכה
sources.says: Maimonides opens his account of what makes a well-made parable with this verse.

25:11.headline: A word spoken, or a word driven along
25:11.body: דבר דבר looks like "a word spoken". Ibn Ezra reads the second דבר through Aramaic, where the same root means to lead a flock, so the word is driven along on its proper wheels.

sources.quote: דבור - תרגום וינהג, כלומר נהוג על אפניו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this word is the Aramaic for 'he led', so it means a word led along on its wheels.

25:11.headline: A word on its wheels, or a word set in its place
25:11.body: Metzudat Zion ties אפניו to אופן, a wheel, and Metzudat David says a fitting word comes back around like a turning wheel. Rashi rejects the wheel reading because of the vowels, and says it means a word set firmly in place.

sources.quote: אפניו. מל׳ אופן עגלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from the wheel of a cart.

sources.quote: וחוזרת אליו כאופן העגלה המתגלגל וחוזר למקומו
sources.says: Metzudat David says a fitting word comes back to its subject like a cart wheel rolling back to its place.

sources.quote: וְאֵין זֶה מִגִּזְרַת ׳אוֹפַן וְגַלְגַּל׳
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'on its base', and is not from the word for wheel, since the vowels would then be different.

25:13.headline: The cool of snow, or a shield against the heat
25:13.body: Rashi says this is the coolness of snowy days that a harvester longs for, not real snow, which would spoil the harvest. Ibn Ezra adds that it may come from צנה, a shield, because it guards the harvester from the heat.

sources.quote: וְלֹא שֶׁלֶג מַמָּשׁ, שֶׁהַשֶּׁלֶג לֹא טוֹב הוּא בִּשְׁעַת קָצִיר
sources.says: Rashi says it means the cold of snowy days, not actual snow, since snow is bad at harvest time.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיותו מן צנה וסוחרה, בעבור שהגין על האדם בעת קציר מפני החום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means coolness, or perhaps comes from צנה, a shield, since it protects a person from the heat at harvest.

sources.quote: כצנת. מל׳ צנה וקור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is from a word for cold.

25:14.headline: These "princes" are rain clouds
25:14.body: נשיאים usually means princes. Here it means clouds: Metzudat Zion says they lift themselves up, and Ibn Ezra says the wind carries them in from the ends of the earth.

sources.quote: נשיאים. עננים ע״ש שמנשאים עצמם למעלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means clouds, named for lifting themselves up high.

sources.quote: נשיאים - נקראו כן העננים, בעבור שינשאו מקצה הארץ ורוח נושאם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says clouds have this name because they are carried from the end of the earth, with the wind bearing them.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהַשָּׁמַיִם מִתְקַשְּׁרִים בֶּעָבִים וְהָרוּחַ מְנַשֶּׁבֶת
sources.says: Rashi pictures the sky tied up with clouds and the wind blowing, yet no rain comes, like a man who boasts of charity and does not give.

25:16.headline: Too much honey, and you lose it all
25:16.body: Maimonides reads this honey as deep knowledge, and stops on the word "vomit": the verse does not say you will grow tired of it, but that you will lose everything, even what you took in.

sources.quote: ואם תהיה בהפרזה יאבד הכול
sources.says: Maimonides compares knowledge to honey, which nourishes in measure but makes one vomit in excess, so that all is lost, and notes the verse says 'vomit' rather than 'loathe'.

sources.quote: פן תקיא את הכל ותאבד גם המעט שאכלת בתחילה
sources.says: Metzudat David says eating too much makes you throw up all of it, losing even the little you ate at first.

25:17.headline: Make your visits rare, and they stay precious
25:17.body: הקר comes from יקר, precious and rare. Metzudat David says a friend seen now and then is loved more, and Maimonides uses the verse to explain why the Temple was not to be entered at all times.

sources.quote: הוקר. מל׳ יקר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from יקר, precious.

sources.quote: כי האוהב הנראה לפרקים אהוב ביותר
sources.says: Metzudat David says a friend who is seen only at times is loved most.

sources.quote: ואמרו שאין רצוי להיכנס למקדש בכל עת
sources.says: Maimonides says the Sages used this verse to teach that one should not enter the Temple at all times, so it keeps its awe.

25:17.headline: Your friend's house may be God's house
25:17.body: Plainly the verse warns against wearing out a friend's welcome. Rashi brings the Sages' reading that the friend is God, so a person should not keep sinning and bringing offerings to his house.

sources.quote: וּלְהָבִיא תָּמִיד חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת לְבֵית ה׳ שֶׁנִּקְרָא רֵעַ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi brings the Sages' reading: do not get used to sinning and always bringing sin offerings to God's house, since God is called Israel's friend in the Song of Songs.

sources.quote: בל יתמיד להביא קרבנות לבית ה' על חטאיו
sources.says: Malbim says the Sages read it as a warning not to keep bringing offerings for one's sins to God's house.

25:20.headline: Taking off a coat, or putting on finery, on a cold day
25:20.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take מעדה from an Aramaic word for removing, so it is a coat taken off, or so worn it should be, on a cold day. Metzudat Zion takes it from עדי, finery, which looks fine but does not keep you warm.

sources.quote: בֶּגֶד מוּסָר, כְּלִי שֶׁהוּא רָאוּי לַהֲסִירוֹ מֵעָלָיו לְפִי שֶׁהוּא בָּלוּי
sources.says: Rashi says it is a garment fit to be taken off because it is worn out, citing the Aramaic word for 'removed'.

sources.quote: מעדה בגד - תרגום ויסר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is the Aramaic for 'he removed'.

sources.quote: מעדה. מל׳ עדי וקשוט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from עדי, jewelry and adornment.

sources.quote: המעלה על גופו בגד מקושט ביום קרה ונחמד הוא למראה העין אבל אין בזה שום תועלת להגן מהקור
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is a fancy garment on a cold day, nice to look at but no help against the cold.

25:20.headline: Natron: soft earth that vinegar eats away
25:20.body: נתר is a rare word for a kind of earth. Rashi says it was soft earth carved into vessels, which vinegar dissolves, while Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra say it was used for washing and crumbles when liquid touches it.

sources.quote: נָתֶר. מִין אֲדָמָה רַכָּה, כְּגוֹן אֲדָמָה שֶׁלָּנוּ הַנִּקְרָא קְרִידָ״א
sources.says: Rashi says it is a soft earth like the one called creda in his own language, carved into vessels that vinegar ruins.

sources.quote: נתר. מין אדמה רכה עשוי לכבס בו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a soft earth used for washing, as in Jeremiah.

sources.quote: ונתר ידוע להתכבס בו, והנה אם המים יפרפרוהו כל שכן החומץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is known for washing, and if water crumbles it, vinegar surely does.

25:20.headline: A "bad heart" here is a broken heart
25:20.body: לב רע usually means an evil heart. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read רע here as broken, like the broken tooth in verse 19, so cheerful songs do not help someone in grief.

sources.quote: רע. מושבר כמו שן רועה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means broken, like the 'broken tooth' of the verse before.

sources.quote: ומלת רע – מן תרועם, כלומר שבור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means broken, and that one should not burden a sick person with songs.

sources.quote: השר בשירי שמחה על לב נשבר
sources.says: Metzudat David speaks of singing happy songs to a broken heart, whose pain stays inside.

25:21.headline: Your hungry enemy may be your own urge to sin
25:21.body: Plainly the verse says to feed an enemy who is hungry, as Ralbag explains. Rashi also brings the Sages' reading that the enemy is the urge to do wrong: when it hungers for sin, feed it the bread of Torah.

sources.quote: לא תמנע מלחון עליו להאכילו לחם
sources.says: Ralbag says do not hold back from being kind to your enemy and feeding him bread.

sources.quote: אִם רָעֵב הוּא וְאוֹמֵר לְךָ לְהַשְׂבִּיעוֹ בַּעֲבֵרוֹת, מְשׁוֹךְ אֶת עַצְמְךָ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi gives the plain sense, then the Sages' reading: if the evil urge is hungry and asks you to fill it with sins, draw yourself to the study house.

25:23.headline: The north wind brings rain, or drives it away
25:23.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read תחולל as giving birth: the north wind brings rain, as gossip brings angry faces. Ibn Ezra offers the opposite, from a root meaning to hold back: the wind scatters the clouds, and an angry face stops the gossip.

sources.quote: תּוֹלִיד וְתִבְרָא אֶת הַגֶּשֶׁם
sources.says: Rashi says the north wind gives birth to and creates the rain.

sources.quote: תחולל. ענין בריאה והולדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means creating and giving birth.

sources.quote: והוא מן חלילה כלומר תמנע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word may mean 'holds back', so the north wind keeps rain from falling, and an angry face keeps a gossip from talking.

25:27.headline: Searching out their honor: an honor, or not?
25:27.body: The second half of the verse is terse. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as praise: probing the sages' rulings and wisdom is an honor, while Ralbag carries over the "not" from the first half: probing holy things too far is no honor.

sources.quote: בְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים, אֲשֶׁר כְּבוֹדָם כָּבוֹד בִּגְזֵרוֹתֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the place for probing is the words of the sages, whose rulings one may ask the reasons for.

sources.quote: מהראוי להרבות לחקור חכמתם שהיא כבודם ותפארתם
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is right to search deeply into the wisdom of the righteous, which is their honor.

sources.quote: כי ההרבו' בחקר כבוד' אינו כבוד
sources.says: Ralbag says too much probing of holy knowledge is no honor, since the human mind cannot fully grasp it.

26:2.headline: A baseless curse will not land, or will fly back home
26:2.body: The word is written לא, "it will not come", and read לו, "it will come to him". Malbim reads both: by the written form the curse never arrives, and by the read form it returns to the one who said it, as Rashi also explains.

sources.quote: לו תבוא, שתשוב אל המקלל
sources.says: Malbim says that by the written form the curse does not come at all, and by the read form it returns to the one who cursed, like birds flying back to their nest.

sources.quote: כֵּן קִלְלַת חִנָּם לוֹ תָבוֹא. לְמִי שֶׁהוֹצִיאָהּ בְּפִיו
sources.says: Rashi says a baseless curse comes back to the one who said it.

sources.quote: כן קללת חנם חוזרים ובאים אל המקלל עצמו
sources.says: Metzudat David says baseless curses come back to the curser himself.

26:2.headline: Swallow or bat: the bird named for freedom
26:2.body: Rashi says the דרור is the swallow, named because it dwells, דרה, in a house as freely as in a field. Metzudat Zion calls it a bat, named from דרור, freedom, since it nests in houses as if free of people.

sources.quote: וְנִקְרָא דְּרוֹר – שֶׁדָּרָה בַּבַּיִת כְּבַשָּׂדֶה
sources.says: Rashi gives the bird's Old French name, the swallow, and says it is named for dwelling in a house as in a field.

sources.quote: ותקרא דרור ע״ש שמקננת בבתים כאלו היתה חפשית מבני אדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a bat, called דרור because it nests in houses as if it were free of people, since דרור means freedom.

26:6.headline: Sending a fool cuts off your own feet
26:6.body: Metzudat Zion reads מקצה as cutting off, and Ibn Ezra also offers "pushing his feet to the edge". Rashi says sending a fool wears out the feet of the messengers you must send after him to fix his mistakes.

sources.quote: מקצה. מל׳ קציצה וכתיתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means cutting and crushing.

sources.quote: ופירוש: מקצה מרחיק אל הקצה רגליו ואינו הולך לצרכו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, from קצה, edge: he pushes his feet off to the side and does not get where he needs to go.

sources.quote: הוּא מְקַצֶּה רַגְלֵי שְׁלוּחִים הַרְבֵּה, לַחֲזוֹר וְלִשְׁלֹחַ לְתַקֵּן מַה שֶּׁעִוֵּת הָרִאשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says he wears out the feet of many messengers, sent again and again to fix what the first one spoiled.

26:7.headline: To a lame man, everyone's legs look tall
26:7.body: דליו is a rare word that Rashi reads as "raised": to a lame man everyone's legs look high, and the fool says wisdom is just as far out of reach. Ibn Ezra also suggests "thinned", from a related root.

sources.quote: הַשּׁוֹקַיִם שֶׁל כָּל אָדָם נִרְאִין לַפִּסֵּחַ גְּבוֹהִים מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says everyone's legs look higher to the lame man, and a fool uses this saying to claim wisdom is too high for him.

sources.quote: דליו. ענין הרמה כמו דלו עיני למרום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means raising, as in Isaiah, 'my eyes are lifted up'.

sources.quote: פרוש אחר: דליו - כמו דללו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, 'grew thin'.

26:10.headline: The Great One who made all, or a brawler who wounds all
26:10.body: This verse is hard. Rashi and Malbim read רב as God, the Master who creates everything, while Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read רב as a quarrelsome man and מחולל as one who wounds.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּרָא אֶת הַכֹּל וְדָן אֶת הַכֹּל
sources.says: Rashi says it means God, who created all and judges all.

sources.quote: רב תואר לה' יתברך, שהוא רב ואדון על הכל
sources.says: Malbim says רב is a title for God, master over everything.

sources.quote: רב. מל׳ מריבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רב comes from quarreling.

sources.quote: איש ריב ירבה חללים
sources.says: Metzudat David says a quarrelsome man leaves many wounded.

26:10.headline: The fool, or the star called Kesil
26:10.body: כסיל usually means a fool. Rashi brings a midrash that reads it as the star Kesil and reads שוכר as סוכר, to close off: God shuts down that star, and from then closes the sea to sailors until Passover.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא סוֹכֵר מַזַּל כְּסִיל
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash reading שוכר as 'closes off', like the closing of the springs in the flood story: God closes off the star Kesil and shuts the sea to travelers until Passover.

26:16.headline: Wiser than seven: the king's seven advisers
26:16.body: The lazy man thinks himself wiser than seven who give sound answers. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David suggest these are the king's inner circle, those who see the king's face.

sources.quote: משבעה - יתכן שהם רואי פני המלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the seven may be those who see the king's face.

sources.quote: יותר משבעה רואי פני המלך היודעים להשיב טעם
sources.says: Metzudat David says the lazy man thinks himself wiser than the king's seven advisers, who can answer any question.

sources.quote: מְשִׁיבֵי טָעַם. חֲכָמִים
sources.says: Rashi says those who give answers are the wise.

26:17.headline: Who is passing by: the meddler or the dog?
26:17.body: Rashi reads עבר with the meddler: a passer-by who gets worked up over someone else's fight. Malbim attaches it to the dog: grabbing the ears of a dog that was just passing by and had not barked at you.

sources.quote: הָעוֹבֵר לְהִתְעַבֵּר עַל רִיב לֹא לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says one who passes by and gets involved in a fight not his own is like one who grabs a dog's ears.

sources.quote: ומתעבר – כועס במריבה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מתעבר means getting angry in a quarrel.

sources.quote: מי שמחזיק באזני כלב שעובר לדרכו ולא נבח עליו
sources.says: Malbim says it is a dog going on its way that had not barked at him, until he grabbed its ears.

26:18.headline: A madman, a weary man, or a prankster
26:18.body: כמתלהלה is a rare word. Metzudat Zion reads it as one who wears himself out, Ibn Ezra as one who acts mad, and Malbim as a prankster, from התל, mocking, with the letters reversed.

sources.quote: כמתלהלה. ענין יגיעה ועייפות כמו ותלה ארץ מצרים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means toil and weariness, as when Egypt grew faint in the famine.

sources.quote: כמתלהלה - כמשתטה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means like one who acts mad.

sources.quote: כמתלהלה. שרשו תלה כמו התל בהפך אתוון, המהתל בחברו
sources.says: Malbim says the root is התל with letters reversed: one who mocks his friend.

sources.quote: כְּמִתְיַגֵּעַ לִירוֹת זִיקִים שֶׁל אֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it is like one who toils to shoot sparks of fire.

26:22.headline: A gossip's words: blows, or death to those who hear
26:22.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read כמתלהמים as blows that break. Rashi also brings the Sages' play on its sounds, כמת להם, "like death to them": the spies' report was death to those who heard it.

sources.quote: כמתלהמים. ענין הכאה המשברת והוא הפוך מן יהלמני צדיק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means crushing blows, from the root הלם with letters swapped.

sources.quote: פירוש: כמכים כן דברי הנרגן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the gossip's words are like blows.

sources.quote: כְּמִתְלַהֲמִים: כְּמֵת לָהֶם. דִּבְרֵי הַמְרַגְּלִים הָיוּ לָהֶם לְמִיתָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'like fighters', then brings the Sages' reading 'like death to them': the spies' words were death to them.

26:23.headline: Burning lips, or lips that chase after you
26:23.body: דלק usually means to burn. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it here as chasing, as when Jacob says Laban "hotly pursued" him, while Ibn Ezra keeps the sense of burning, lips that glow like silver.

sources.quote: דּוֹלְקִים. כְּמוֹ ״דָּלַקְתָּ אַחֲרָי״
sources.says: Rashi says it means pursuing, as Jacob says to Laban 'you hotly pursued me'.

sources.quote: דולקים. ענין רדיפה כמו דלקת אחרי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pursuit.

sources.quote: דולקים - מן דלקת והזכיר הכסף, כי לבת הדולקת היא שמדמה אליו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is from burning, and silver is mentioned because burning lips shine like it.

26:24.headline: A hater disguises himself, or gives himself away
26:24.body: The root נכר can mean to disguise or to recognize. Rashi and Malbim say the hater hides behind friendly words, while the Targum and Ibn Ezra read it the other way: his lips give his hatred away.

sources.quote: בְּדִבּוּרוֹ מִתְנַכֵּר הַשּׂוֹנֵא, שֶׁלֹּא יַכִּירוּ שֶׁהוּא שׂוֹנֵא
sources.says: Rashi says the hater disguises himself with his speech so that no one recognizes he is an enemy.

sources.quote: ינכר. הפך ההכרה, כמו ויתנכר אליהם
sources.says: Malbim says it is the opposite of recognition, as when Joseph disguised himself to his brothers.

sources.quote: מַן שִׂפְוָתֵיהּ מִתְיְדַע סָנְאָה
sources.says: The Targum translates 'by his lips the hater is known'.

sources.quote: ככסף שהוא נכר כשהוא מצופה על החרס
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that as silver is recognized when plated on clay, so the hater is recognized by his burning lips.

26:25.headline: Seven abominations: many, or the seven God hates
26:25.body: Metzudat Zion says seven here just means many. Ibn Ezra says they are the seven things God hates, listed in chapter 6.

sources.quote: שבע. ר״ל הרבה וכן שבע יפול צדיק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says seven means many, as in 'a righteous man falls seven times'.

sources.quote: והם הנזכרים למעלה בפסוק שש הנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the abominations God hates, listed earlier in the verse 'six things the Lord hates'.

26:26.headline: Hatred hidden in the dark
26:26.body: משאון is a rare word. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as darkness: what is done in hiding, God will expose in public. Ibn Ezra reads it as ruin: fear of ruin makes him hide his hatred.

sources.quote: הָעוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשָׂיו בַּמַּחְשָׁךְ וּמְכַסֶּה בְּמַשָּׁאוֹן, שֶׁהוּא חֹשֶׁךְ
sources.says: Rashi says it means darkness: one who acts in the dark will in the end be exposed by God in public.

sources.quote: במשאון. בחושך כמו אמש שואה ומשואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means in darkness, as in a phrase in Job.

sources.quote: בעבור משאון שיבואהו יכסה ויעלים השנאה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the hater hides his hatred because of the ruin that would come on him.

26:27.headline: Roll a stone and it rolls back: Abimelech's end
26:27.body: Rashi says this is anyone who sets a stumbling block for others. He also brings a midrash: Abimelech killed his seventy brothers on one stone, and died when a woman dropped a millstone on his head.

sources.quote: סוֹפוֹ שֶׁל הַמַּעֲמִיד מִכְשׁוֹל, שֶׁיִּכָּשֵׁל בּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says one who sets up a stumbling block will in the end stumble on it.

sources.quote: בַּאֲבִימֶלֶךְ שֶׁהָרַג שִׁבְעִים אֶחָיו עַל אֶבֶן אַחַת, וְסוֹף מֵת בָּאֶבֶן
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash about Abimelech, who killed his seventy brothers on one stone and in the end died by a stone, as told in Judges 9.

26:28.headline: A lying tongue hates the people it crushes
26:28.body: Ralbag says a liar comes to hate the very people his lies have crushed, and Rashi points to Saul, who hunted David and destroyed Nob because of slander. The Targum reads it as a lying tongue hating the ways of truth.

sources.quote: איש לשון שקר ישנא הנדכאים בשקריו
sources.says: Ralbag says a liar hates the people crushed by his lies, even though they did him no harm.

sources.quote: מִי שֶׁמְּקַבֵּל לָשׁוֹן הָרָע שׂוֹנֵא אֶת הַנִּדְכָּאִים תַּחְתָּיו
sources.says: Rashi says one who accepts slander hates those crushed beneath him, as Saul pursued David and killed the priests of Nob.

sources.quote: לִישָׁנָא דְשִׁקְרָא סָנֵי אָרְחֲתָא דְקוּשְׁטָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'a lying tongue hates the ways of truth'.

27:6.headline: An enemy's kisses come in heaps, and weigh on you
27:6.body: The root עתר usually means to plead, as when Isaac pleaded for Rebecca. Rashi says it also means a great amount, so an enemy's kisses seem plentiful but are only a burden.

sources.quote: וְנַעְתָּרוֹת. לְשׁוֹן גֹּדֶל, כְּמוֹ ״הַעְתַּרְתֶּם עָלַי״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means 'much', as in Ezekiel's 'you multiplied your words against me'.

sources.quote: דּוֹמוֹת לִמְרֻבּוֹת וְהִנָּם לְמַשָּׂא
sources.says: On Isaac's prayer, Rashi says every use of עתר means pressing and plenty, and that an enemy's kisses seem many but are a burden.

sources.quote: ופירוש נעתרות עבות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra explains the word as 'thick'.

27:8.headline: A midrash reads the wandering man as God leaving His home
27:8.body: Rashi reads the man who strays from his place as a student who drifts from his studies. A midrash that Radak quotes reads him as God, whose place is the Temple, wandering away when Israel went into exile.

sources.quote: ואין איש אלא הקדוש ברוך הוא
sources.says: Radak cites a midrash: the 'man' in this verse is God, as in 'the LORD is a man of war', and His place is the Temple.

sources.quote: תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הַנּוֹדֵד מִן הַלִּמּוּד, מִלַּחֲזֹר עַל גִּרְסָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is a scholar who wanders from study and does not go back over what he learned.

27:10.headline: Your father's friend: Rashi says it is God
27:10.body: רֵעַ means a friend or neighbor. Rashi reads "your friend and your father's friend" as God, and he reads Hillel's rule "what is hateful to you, do not do to your friend" the same way, citing this verse.

sources.quote: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁנִּקְרָא רֵעַ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the friend is God, who is called Israel's friend, and your father's friend because He loved your ancestors.

sources.quote: זה הקב"ה אל תעבור על דבריו
sources.says: Explaining Hillel's rule about your friend, Rashi cites this verse and says the friend is God: do not break His word.

27:14.headline: Praising a friend loudly every morning can work as a curse
27:14.body: Metzudat Zion says the word here means singing someone's praises. Rashi, following the Talmud, explains the curse: praise of a friend's wealth and generosity brings beggars and the government to his door.

sources.quote: מברך. ענין התפארות כמו אשר המתברך בארץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means glorifying, as in a verse in Isaiah.

sources.quote: שֶׁאוֹמְרִים עָלָיו שֶׁהוּא וַתְרָן בְּמָמוֹנוֹ וְעָשִׁיר, וְהַכֹּל בָּאִין וְשׁוֹאֲלִין מִמֶּנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says people then call him generous and rich, everyone comes to ask him for things, and the government goes after his money, as the Talmud explains.

27:15.headline: The dripping roof does not just bother you, it drives you out
27:15.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read טורד through Aramaic, where the root means to drive away. Metzudat David pictures the family chased from spot to spot by the leak, the way a quarrelsome wife gives no rest.

sources.quote: טורד - מגרש, תרגום: ויגרשום וטרדינון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'drives out', the word the Aramaic translation uses for 'they drove them out'.

sources.quote: טורד. ענין גרושין כמו ולך טרדין
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means driving out, as in Daniel's 'they will drive you away'.

sources.quote: ויטריד בני הבית ממקום למקום
sources.says: Metzudat David says the dripping rain chases the household from place to place.

27:15.headline: A rainy day named for the doors everyone shuts
27:15.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion link the rare word סגריר to סגר, to shut, since on a rainy day everyone stays shut indoors. Ibn Ezra notes its doubled last letter and says the rain itself may be called סגריר.

sources.quote: יוֹם הַגֶּשֶׁם, שֶׁהַכֹּל נִסְגָּרִים בְּבָתֵּיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is a day of rain, when everyone is shut in their houses.

sources.quote: סגריר. מל׳ סגירה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from shutting.

sources.quote: כפול הלמ"ד על משקל זרזיף, כלומר ביום שיסגרו בני אדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the last root letter is doubled, and it is the day people shut themselves in, or else the name of the rain.

27:16.headline: Hiding the wind, or the harsh north wind?
27:16.body: צפן means to hide, and צפון is the north. Rashi reads "whoever hides her hides the wind", while the Aramaic Targum reads the words as the harsh north wind.

sources.quote: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִצְפֹּן הָרוּחַ, כֵּן הִיא, לֹא תִצָּפֵנֶה
sources.says: Rashi says that just as you cannot hide the wind, you cannot hide her away.

sources.quote: רוּחָא גַרְבַיְתָא קַשְׁיָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'the north wind is harsh'.

27:17.headline: "Face" here may mean anger
27:17.body: פנים usually means a face. Ibn Ezra reads it here as anger, as in "the face of the LORD scattered them", so a man grows sharp for a fight because of his friend's fury.

sources.quote: ונקרא הזעם פנים, בעבור שיראה בהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says anger is called 'face' because it shows there, as in 'the face of the LORD scattered them'.

sources.quote: שהוא מחדד לריב עמו בעבור חמות רעהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the man sharpens himself to quarrel because of his friend's anger.

27:19.headline: Water shows your own face back, or no two faces match
27:19.body: Rashi and Metzudat David read the water as a mirror: the face you bring is the face you get back, and so with hearts. The Aramaic Targum reads it the other way: no two faces are alike, and neither are people's hearts.

sources.quote: הַלָּלוּ הַפָּנִים שֶׁאַתָּה מַרְאֶה לְתוֹכָן, הֵן מַרְאוֹת לְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the face you show into the water is the face it shows you.

sources.quote: אם שוחקות שוחקות ואם עצבות עצבות
sources.says: Metzudat David says a smiling face comes back smiling and a sad one sad.

sources.quote: הֵיךְ פַּרְצוּפֵי דְלָא דָמְיָן חַד לְחָד
sources.says: The Targum says faces are not like one another, and so people's hearts are not alike.

27:22.headline: The pestle is called עלי because it is lifted
27:22.body: עֱלִי, a pestle, is a rare word. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is named for going up, since it is raised and brought down again and again.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁמַּעֲלִין אוֹתוֹ וּמַכִּין בּוֹ תָּמִיד נִקְרָא עֱלִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is called עלי because it is raised and struck with all the time.

sources.quote: וקרויה כן ע״ש שמעלין ומורידין אותה בעת הכתישה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the pestle is named for being raised and lowered while pounding, citing this verse.

27:22.headline: Pounded grain, named for being loosened from its husk
27:22.body: הריפות is a rare word for grain pounded in a mortar. Metzudat Zion reads it from רפה, to loosen, because the grains are loosened and peeled from their husks.

sources.quote: הָרִיפוֹת. חִטִּים הַנִּדּוֹכִים בַּמַּכְתֵּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it is wheat crushed in a mortar.

sources.quote: מל׳ רפיון ור״ל החטים הנרפים הנקלפים מקליפותיהן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from loosening: wheat loosened and peeled from its husks.

27:23.headline: Know your flock: a rabbi's community, or what the senses take in
27:23.body: Read plainly, the closing verses tell a farmer to tend his sheep. Rashi applies them to a rabbi caring for his community, while Ralbag reads the flock as what the senses take in, from which the mind learns.

sources.quote: פְּנֵי צֹאנְךָ – הָרַב הַמִּתְמַנֶּה עַל הַצִּבּוּר
sources.says: Rashi applies 'the face of your flock' to the rabbi appointed over a community, who should carry them gently.

sources.quote: דע פני צאנך והם המוחשו
sources.says: Ralbag says the flock is the things the senses perceive, from which a person gains knowledge.

28:3.headline: A 'poor man' who is poor in learning, not money
28:3.body: רש means a poor man. Rashi reads it as a judge who is poor in learning. Because he rushes his rulings, he ruins the weak like a rain that washes the field away.

sources.quote: גֶּבֶר רָשׁ. דַּיָּן עַם הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says the poor man is an ignorant judge.

sources.quote: עַל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מָתוּן בְּדִין, הֲרֵי הוּא כְּמָטָר הַסּוֹחֵף אֶת הַשָּׂדֶה
sources.says: Rashi says that because he is not careful in judgment, he is like a rain that sweeps the field away.

28:7.headline: A shepherd of gluttons, or their friend?
28:7.body: רועה usually means a shepherd. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it from רע, a friend: the son who keeps company with gluttons shames his father.

sources.quote: מְחַבֵּר לוֹ זוֹלְלִים, וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן רֵעִים
sources.says: Rashi says he joins himself to gluttons, and the word means friends.

sources.quote: ורועה. ענין חבור וריעות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means joining and friendship.

sources.quote: ורועה - מן רעה המלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the word used for 'the king's friend'.

28:15.headline: A growling bear, or a bear that tramples?
28:15.body: שוקק describes the bear. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is the bear's cry, as נוהם is the lion's growl. Ibn Ezra ties it to שוק, the leg: a bear that tramples, like a wicked ruler over the poor.

sources.quote: נְהִימָה לַאֲרִי וּשְׁקִיקָה לַדֹּב, שְׁנֵיהֶם לְשׁוֹן צְעָקָה
sources.says: Rashi says the lion's sound is נהימה and the bear's is שקיקה, and both mean a cry.

sources.quote: שאגת הארי נקרא נהימה ושאגת הדוב שקיקה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the lion's roar is called נהימה and the bear's roar שקיקה.

sources.quote: שוקק - מן שוק, כלומר דורס
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from שוק, the leg, meaning it tramples.

28:23.headline: Rebuke 'after me', or favor that comes later?
28:23.body: אחרי can mean 'after me' or 'afterward'. Ibn Ezra reads it as Solomon speaking: one who rebukes by my teaching. Rashi and Ralbag read 'later on': in the end, the one who rebukes wins more favor than the flatterer.

sources.quote: מי שיוכיח אדם אחר מצותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means one who rebukes a person following Solomon's commands.

sources.quote: לְאַחַר זְמַן חֵן יִמְצָא בְּעֵינָיו יוֹתֵר מִמַּחֲלִיק לָשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says after a while he finds more favor in the man's eyes than a flatterer does.

sources.quote: או תהיה היו"ד באחרי נוספת
sources.says: Ralbag says the letter yod in אחרי may be extra, so it means 'afterward'.

28:25.headline: Stirring up strife, or stirring up God's judgment
28:25.body: מדון means strife. Rashi hears דין, judgment, in it: the greedy man stirs up God's strict judgment against himself.

sources.quote: יגרה. מל׳ תגר ומריבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the phrase is about quarrels and strife.

sources.quote: מְגָרֶה עָלָיו מִדַּת הַדִּין
sources.says: Rashi says he stirs up God's strict judgment against himself.

29:3.headline: Friend of prostitutes, or the man who feeds them
29:3.body: The word ורעה can come from רע, a friend, or from רעה, to graze and feed. So the man either keeps company with prostitutes or pays to keep them.

sources.quote: ורועה - מן רעך, או מענין: כמרעיתם וישבעו, כלומר מפרנס הזונות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives both roots: a friend, or one who feeds and supports the prostitutes.

sources.quote: ורועה. מל׳ ריעות וחבור
sources.says: Metzudat Zion reads it as friendship and keeping company.

29:3.headline: The Sages hear 'this one is nice' inside the word for prostitutes
29:3.body: The Sages read זונות as if it said זו נאה, 'this one is nice', about a student who studies only the teachings he likes. Rashi backs this up: only here in Scripture is זונות spelled out in full.

sources.quote: הָאוֹמֵר שְׁמוּעָה זוֹ נָאָה – אֶשְׁנֶנָּה, וְזוֹ אֵינָהּ נָאָה – לֹא אֶשְׁנֶנָּה
sources.says: Rashi brings the Sages' reading: the one who says 'this teaching is nice, I will learn it; this one is not, I will not'.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין ״זוֹנוֹת״ בַּמִּקְרָא מָלֵא אֶלָּא זֶה בִּלְבַד
sources.says: Rashi notes that זונות is spelled in full only in this verse, which supports the reading.

29:5.headline: Smooth words, or a slippery road
29:5.body: Rashi reads מחליק as speaking smooth, flattering words. Metzudat David reads it as making the road slick so a friend will slip, and the trap then catches the one who set it.

sources.quote: מַחֲלִיק. מְדַבֵּר חֲלָקוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means one who speaks smooth words.

sources.quote: מי שמחליק את הדרך למען ימעדו בה רגלי רעהו
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is one who makes the road slippery so his friend's feet will slip.

29:11.headline: Not 'praise' but 'calm', as God stills the roaring sea
29:11.body: The root שבח usually means to praise. Here the commentators read it as 'quiet it down', the same verb Psalms uses for God calming the noise of the seas.

sources.quote: ישבחנה. ענין השפלה והשקטה כמו משביח שאון ימים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means lowering and calming, as in 'who stills the roar of the seas'.

sources.quote: ישבחנה - מן משביח שאון, פירוש ישקיט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from 'stills the roar' and means to quiet.

sources.quote: וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ ״מַשְׁבִּיחַ שְׁאוֹן יַמִּים״
sources.says: Rashi compares it to the verse about stilling the roar of the seas.

29:18.headline: Without prophecy a people runs wild, goes idle, or is exposed
29:18.body: Rashi reads יפרע as breaking through limits, so the people run loose. Metzudat Zion reads it as stopping, and Ibn Ezra as being laid bare.

sources.quote: יִפְרְצוּ בָם פְּרָצוֹת וְיוֹצְאִין לְתַרְבּוּת רָעָה
sources.says: Rashi says breaches open in them and they turn to bad ways.

sources.quote: יפרע. ענין השבתה ובטול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means ceasing and being idle.

sources.quote: אז יפרע עם ויגלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the people is uncovered.

29:22.headline: An angry man stirs up quarrels, or God's strict judgment
29:22.body: Rashi first takes מדון plainly, as a quarrel between people. He then also reads it as מדת הדין, God's strict justice, which the angry man stirs up.

sources.quote: כְּמַשְׁמָעוֹ. מָדוֹן מִדַּת הַדִּין
sources.says: Rashi says the verse means what it says, and that מדון is the attribute of strict judgment.

3:8.headline: A drink for your bones means the marrow inside them
3:8.body: שקוי usually means a drink. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it means the marrow, which waters the bones from inside, as a verse in Job puts it.

sources.quote: הוּא הַמֹּחַ, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וּמֹחַ עַצְמוֹתָיו יְשֻׁקֶּה״
sources.says: Rashi says it is the marrow, as Job says 'the marrow of his bones is watered'.

sources.quote: ר״ל המוח המשקה העצמות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the marrow that waters the bones.

3:9.headline: Honor God with your wealth, or with your throat
3:9.body: הון means wealth. Rashi widens it to anything God gave you, even a sweet voice, and brings the Sages' reading of מהונך as מגרונך, 'from your throat'.

sources.quote: מִכָּל מַה שֶּׁחֲנָנְךָ, אֲפִלּוּ מִקּוֹל עָרֵב. (אַל תִּקְרִי מֵהוֹנֶךָ אֶלָּא מִגְּרוֹנֶךָ)
sources.says: Rashi says it means from whatever God granted you, even a pleasant voice, and gives the reading 'do not read from your wealth but from your throat'.

3:12.headline: A father who makes up with his son, or makes him whole
3:12.body: Rashi reads ירצה as a father who wants good for his son and makes peace with him after punishing him. Meiri, writing on Psalms, reads it instead as making whole, as in a verse in Leviticus about the land making up its lost rest years.

sources.quote: שֶׁרוֹצֶה בִּבְנוֹ לְהֵיטִיב לוֹ וִיפַיְּסֵהוּ לְאַחַר שֶׁמַּכֵּהוּ בַּשֵּׁבֶט
sources.says: Rashi says the father wants to do his son good and makes up with him after striking him with the rod.

sources.quote: ירצה. מלשון רצוי ופיוס
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means pleasing and making peace.

sources.quote: או נפרש כי השלמתם מלשון והרצת את שבתותיה (ויקר׳ כז לד) וכן לדעתי וכאב את בן ירצה
sources.says: Meiri says the root can mean to complete, as in the land making up its sabbaths, and that in his view this verse uses it that way.

3:14.headline: In this trade both sides walk away with everything
3:14.body: סחר means trade. Rashi says in a normal trade each side gives something up, but when two people teach each other, both end up with both lessons. Ralbag says a trader travels from land to land, and it is better to travel like that for wisdom.

sources.quote: אֲבָל הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ: שְׁנֵה לִי פִּרְקְךָ וַאֲנִי אֶשְׁנֶה לְךָ פִּרְקִי, נִמְצְאוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּיַד כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says that when one person says to another 'teach me your chapter and I will teach you mine', each ends up holding both.

sources.quote: הנה הסוחר הוא המסבב בארצות לבקש דבר הסחור
sources.says: Ralbag says a trader is one who goes around the lands looking for goods to buy.

3:15.headline: "Your treasures" here mean jewels; plain "treasures" elsewhere mean good deeds
3:15.body: This verse says 'all your treasures' cannot match wisdom, and Proverbs 8:11 says 'all treasures'. Maimonides quotes the Sages: your treasures are jewels and pearls, the other treasures are good deeds, and neither matches knowing God.

sources.quote: חֲפָצִים' – אלו מצות ומעשים טובים, 'חֲפָצֶיךָ' – אלו אבנים טובות ומרגליות
sources.says: Maimonides quotes the midrash: 'treasures' are commandments and good deeds, and 'your treasures' are precious stones and pearls.

sources.quote: חפציך - כל דבר שתחפוץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means anything you desire.

3:16.headline: Right hand and left hand stand for two kinds of students
3:16.body: Rashi reads 'in her right hand' as people who study for its own sake. They get long life. People who study for other reasons are 'the left'. They still get wealth and honor.

sources.quote: לַמְּיַמִּינִים בָּהּ וְעוֹסְקִים בָּהּ לִשְׁמָהּ, אֹרֶךְ יָמִים
sources.says: Rashi says those who go to the right with it and study it for its own sake get long life.

sources.quote: וְלַמַּשְׂמִאילִים בָּהּ, שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בָּהּ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עֹשֶׁר וְכָבוֹד יֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says those who go to the left with it, studying for other reasons, still have wealth and honor.

3:26.headline: God is your trust, or God guards you where you are foolish
3:26.body: כסל can mean trust or hope, and Metzudat Zion reads it that way. Rashi gives that reading and a second one he found in the Jerusalem Talmud: God guards you in the things where you are a fool, כסיל.

sources.quote: בְּמִבְטַחֲךָ. דָּבָר אַחֵר: בַּדְּבָרִים שֶׁאַתָּה כְּסִיל בָּהֶן. כָּךְ מָצָאתִי בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'your trust', or else 'in the matters where you are foolish', a reading he found in the Jerusalem Talmud.

sources.quote: בכסלך. ענין בטחון ותקוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means trust and hope.

3:29.headline: Do not plow evil: plotting pictured as plowing
3:29.body: תחרש here means to plot. Rashi says it keeps the sense of plowing. A plowman readies the ground for sowing, and a plotter readies his schemes in his heart.

sources.quote: אַל תַּחְשֹׁב. וְאֵינוֹ זָז מִמַּשְׁמָעוּת חֲרִישָׁה: מַה דֶּרֶךְ הַחוֹרֵשׁ – מֵכִין מָקוֹם לִזְמַן הַזְּרִיעָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'do not plan', and that it keeps the sense of plowing: the plowman prepares a place for the time of sowing.

sources.quote: תחרוש. ענין מחשבה כמו חורשי און
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means thinking, as in 'those who plow wickedness'.

3:35.headline: Fools set aside shame as their own share
3:35.body: מרים usually means to lift up. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it like תרומה, a portion set aside: each fool sets aside shame as his share. Ralbag also reads it as lifting shame onto oneself.

sources.quote: מרים. מלשון תרומה והפרשה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from setting aside a portion, like terumah.

sources.quote: לְעַצְמוֹ מַפְרִישׁ קָלוֹן לְחֶלְקוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the fool sets aside shame as his own portion.

sources.quote: שכל אחד מהכסילים מרים ומגביה הקלון עליו
sources.says: Ralbag says each fool raises shame up onto himself.

3:35.headline: Shame burns: the word may come from roasting in fire
3:35.body: קלון means disgrace. Metzudat Zion says it may come from קלוי, roasted, because shame makes the face go red as if scorched. Or it may come from being made light of.

sources.quote: בזיון והוא מלשון קלוי באש (ויקרא ב׳:י״ד) כי בעבור הבזיון יתאדם הפנים כאלו נקלה באש, או הוא מלשון קלות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means disgrace, from 'roasted in fire' because shame reddens the face as if burned, or from lightness.

30:1.headline: Son of Yakeh: of one who spat wisdom out
30:1.body: Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David hear יקה as vomiting: Solomon gathered so much understanding that he spat out his gift of prophecy. Ralbag reads it as spitting out wrong ideas to keep the true ones, and Ibn Ezra reports a reading from יקהת עמים, "the gathering of nations".

sources.quote: יקה. מל׳ הקאה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the name comes from vomiting.

sources.quote: ובעבור מרבית הבינה הקיא את הנבואה כי נטלה ממנו
sources.says: Metzudat David says that because of his great understanding Solomon spat out prophecy, which was taken from him.

sources.quote: ורוצה להקיא המעמס והמשא מן המחשבות הבלתי צודקות
sources.says: Ralbag says the name means one who wants to spit out the load of wrong thoughts, so only the right ones remain.

sources.quote: פרוש אחר: בן יקה - בן יקהת עמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a reading that 'son of Yakeh' means son of the one to whom nations gather, a title for Solomon.

30:4.headline: What is his son's name? A family, or a cause
30:4.body: Rashi reads it as a challenge: if someone was like Moses, name his son and his family. Ralbag says thinkers called a nearer cause the "son" of the higher cause behind it, and Malbim says the philosophers called the first thing that flows from God his son.

sources.quote: אִם תֹּאמַר: כְּבָר הָיָה דֻּגְמָתוֹ, אֱמוֹר: מַה שֵּׁם בְּנוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says if you claim there was someone like him, say what his son's name is and what family came from him.

sources.quote: הנה קראו לסבה הקרוב' לזה הפועל בן
sources.says: Ralbag says the nearer cause of an event is called its 'son', because it comes from the higher cause.

sources.quote: שמן העילה הראשונה נאצל עלול ראשון שהוא השכל הנאצל שקראו אותו בשם בן להמאציל העליון
sources.says: Malbim says the questioner followed the philosophers, who called the first intellect flowing from the first cause its 'son'.

30:9.headline: Grabbing God's name: a false oath
30:9.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say a poor man who steals will grab hold of God's name in a false oath, and the Targum translates "profane". Malbim reads it as pinning the name of God on the forces of nature.

sources.quote: לְהַרְגִּיל לְהִשָּׁבַע בּוֹ לַשֶּׁקֶר
sources.says: Rashi says it means getting used to swearing falsely by God's name.

sources.quote: שאשבע על הגנבה, ואתפש בשבועת שם אלהי לשקר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he will swear about the theft and be caught in a false oath by God's name.

sources.quote: וַאֲחַלֵיל שְׁמֵיהּ דֵאלָהָא
sources.says: The Targum translates 'and I will profane the name of God'.

sources.quote: יגנב ויקח לו כחות הטבעיים או כחות הכוכבים ויתפש עליהם שם אלהות
sources.says: Malbim says one poor in understanding steals away the powers of nature or the stars and pins the name of God on them.

30:20.headline: "She ate and wiped her mouth": a polite way to say it
30:20.body: Rashi says "ate" is a clean word used in place of a cruder one. Ibn Ezra reads it as a comparison: as someone wipes food from her mouth so no one knows she ate, so she hides her act.

sources.quote: אָכְלָה. לָשׁוֹן נְקִיָּה דִּבֵּר הַכָּתוּב
sources.says: Rashi says the verse used a clean word.

sources.quote: וכאשר אכלה ומחתה מאכל מפיה, כדי שלא תדע שאכלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says as she eats and wipes the food from her mouth so it is not known she ate, so she sins and denies it.

30:31.headline: King Alkum, or a king no one can stand against
30:31.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra split אלקום into אל קום, "none rise": a king whom no one can stand against. Malbim, in his plain reading, takes Alkum as a king's name, and Rashi admits he does not know its plain sense.

sources.quote: אלקום. המלה ההיא מורכבת משנים אל קום ר״ל אין עומד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is made of 'no' and 'rise': no one stands against him.

sources.quote: כלומר שאין אדם קום להלחם עמו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means no one rises to fight him.

sources.quote: המשל הרביעי המליצו על העבד שמלך שהיה שמו מלך אלקום
sources.says: Malbim, in his plain reading, says this verse was said about a slave who became king, whose name was King Alkum.

sources.quote: וּמֶלֶךְ אַלְקוּם. לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מַה הוּא לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says he does not know what it means in its plain sense.

sources.quote: אַלְקוּם – אֵין עוֹמֵד עִמּוֹ
sources.says: In his midrash reading, Rashi explains Alkum as 'no one stands against him'.

30:33.headline: Squeeze a nose and get blood, squeeze anger and get a fight
30:33.body: The verse plays on one word: אף is a nose, and אפים is anger. Rashi explains that as squeezing the nose too hard brings blood, squeezing anger brings strife.

sources.quote: אפים. מל׳ אף וחימה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אפים comes from anger, while אף earlier in the verse is the nose.

sources.quote: וְדָם עַל יְדֵי מִיץ הַחוֹטֶם יוֹתֵר מִדַּי, כֵּן יֵצֵא רִיב עַל יְדֵי מִיץ אַפַּיִם שֶׁל כַּעַס
sources.says: Rashi says as blood comes from squeezing the nose too much, so strife comes from squeezing anger.

31:1.headline: Lemuel is Solomon, and the name means 'to God'
31:1.body: The commentators say Lemuel is Solomon. Metzudat Zion splits the name into למו אל, 'to God'. Ibn Ezra says he may have been called this because in his day the people served one God and no idols.

sources.quote: לְמוּאֵל לָאֵל, כְּמוֹ ״לְמוֹ פִי״
sources.says: Rashi says Lemuel means 'to God', using למו as in 'to my mouth' in Job.

sources.quote: למואל. המלה ההיא מורכבת משנים למו אל ר״ל אל ה׳
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is made of two words, למו אל, meaning 'to God'.

sources.quote: למואל - הוא שלמה. ויתכן שנקרא כן, כי בימיו היה להם אל אחד ולא עבדו לפסילים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Lemuel is Solomon, perhaps named so because in his days they had one God and did not serve idols.

31:2.headline: A mother calls her son by the Aramaic word, בר
31:2.body: Metzudat Zion says ברי is the Aramaic for 'my son', and Radak uses this verse to explain בר in Psalms 2. Rashi hears a mother's rebuke: what have you done, showing you are my son and not your father's?

sources.quote: ברי. הוא תרגום של בני
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ברי is the Aramaic for 'my son'.

sources.quote: ובר כמו בן; וכן מה ברי ומה בר בטני
sources.says: Radak says בר means son, as in this verse.

sources.quote: מֶה זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ, וְהִגַּדְתָּ שֶׁאַתָּה בְּנִי וְלֹא בֶן אָבִיךָ
sources.says: Rashi has the mother ask what he has done, showing he is her son and not his father's son.

31:4.headline: No strong drink for rulers, or rulers asking 'where is it?'
31:4.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read אי as אין, 'none': strong drink is not fit for rulers. Ralbag reads it as 'where': kings who chase wine and ask, where is the strong drink?

sources.quote: אֵי שֵׁכָר. כְּמוֹ אֵין שֵׁכָר
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'no strong drink'.

sources.quote: אי. כמו אין וכן ימלט אי נקי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אי means 'none', as in a verse in Job.

sources.quote: שרודפים שתיית היין ושואלי' איה שכר לשתותו
sources.says: Ralbag describes kings who chase wine and ask 'where is strong drink to drink?'.

31:6.headline: Give drink to the one who is lost: doomed, or just poor
31:6.body: Rashi reads אובד as someone headed for ruin, the wicked. Ibn Ezra, explaining 'my father was a lost Aramean' in Deuteronomy, says the word means poor, without money, as in this verse.

sources.quote: לְמִי שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְאִבּוּד, לָרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is someone who will end in ruin, the wicked.

sources.quote: והטעם עני בלא ממון וכן תנו שכר לאובד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אובד means poor, without money, as in this verse.

31:8.headline: Orphans, mortals, or muddled speakers: who are בני חלוף
31:8.body: חלוף means passing or changing. Rashi reads בני חלוף as orphans, whose help has passed away. Ibn Ezra reads them as mortals facing a death sentence. Ralbag reads them as people who mix up their words and say the opposite of what they mean.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ הֵן הַיְתוֹמִים, שֶׁחָלְפָה עֶזְרָתָם וְהָלְכָה לָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says these are orphans, whose help has passed away and gone.

sources.quote: בני חלוף - בני תמותה, בעבור משפט המות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are mortals, in a case of life and death.

sources.quote: ובני חלוף הם בעלי התמורה שיאמרו הפך מה שבלבם
sources.says: Ralbag says they are people who switch their words and say the opposite of what is in their heart.

31:15.headline: חק here is not a law but a fixed share of food
31:15.body: חק usually means a law or rule. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say here it means the set portion of food she gives her maids. In Rashi's reading about the Torah, it is the set lesson a teacher gives his students.

sources.quote: וְחֹק. הוּא מָזוֹן הַקָּצוּב לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the food portion set for them.

sources.quote: וחוק - מאכל כענין ואכלו חקם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means food, as in 'they ate their portion'.

sources.quote: שׁוֹנֶה הָרַב לַתַּלְמִידִים הַחֹק הַקָּצוּב לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says, in his reading about the Torah, the teacher teaches his students their set portion.

31:16.headline: She planned for a field, or bridled Esau, man of the field
31:16.body: Plainly זממה means she planned to buy a field, as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say. In his reading about the Torah, Rashi hears זמם, a muzzle: she held back Esau, 'a man of the field', with bit and bridle.

sources.quote: זממה - חשבה לקנות שדה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says she thought about buying a field.

sources.quote: זממה. חשבה כמו כאשר זממתי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means she thought, as in 'as I planned' in Zechariah.

sources.quote: זָמְמָה בְּזֶמֶם וּבְרֶסֶן אֶת ״עֵשָׂו אִישׁ שָׂדֶה״
sources.says: Rashi says she muzzled with bit and bridle Esau, 'a man of the field'.

31:18.headline: She tasted that her trade was good: taste as judgment
31:18.body: טעם means taste, and also good sense. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it here as judgment or counsel. Radak says knowing is called tasting because, as with food, a person tests it for himself, bitter or sweet.

sources.quote: טעמה. ענין עצה כמו וטעם זקנים יקח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means counsel, as in 'he takes away the sense of the elders'.

sources.quote: טעמה - כמו ברוך טעמך, כלומר יעצה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like 'blessed is your good sense', meaning she judged.

sources.quote: כמו שיטעם האדם המאכל ויבחננו בעצמו אם מר, אם מתוק
sources.says: Radak says knowledge is called taste, as a person tastes food and tests for himself whether it is bitter or sweet, and cites this verse.

31:18.headline: A missing letter points to the night of the Exodus
31:18.body: The word is written בליל, without the last letter of 'night'. Rashi says the short spelling points to the 'night of watching' when Egypt was struck. In his reading, the Torah gave Israel light and protection that night.

sources.quote: בְּלֵיל כְּתִיב, חָסֵר ה׳: בְּלֵיל שִׁמּוּרִים שֶׁנִּגְּפוּ הַמִּצְרִיִּים
sources.says: Rashi says it is written בליל, missing the ה, pointing to the night of watching when the Egyptians were struck.

31:19.headline: The spinning tool, and a hint of skill: כישור and כשרון
31:19.body: כישור is a spinning tool, and Metzudat Zion says the word has no match elsewhere. Rashi says it is the part that makes the spindle ready (מכשיר) for spinning. In his Torah reading he hears כשרון, skill.

sources.quote: בכישור. הוא הכלי שהפשחן כרוך בו ואין לו דומה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the tool the flax is wound on, and the word has no parallel.

sources.quote: הַמַּכְשִׁיר אֶת הַפֶּלֶךְ לִטְווֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is the piece that readies the spindle for spinning.

sources.quote: בַּכִּישׁוֹר. בְּכִשְׁרוֹן מַעֲשֶׂיהָ
sources.says: Rashi reads 'with the כישור' as 'with the skill of her deeds'.

31:24.headline: A Canaanite here simply means a merchant
